title: Islam in Africa today
hookLine: the adhan sounds from Dakar to Mombasa, across a continent of Muslims

cards: Dawn on the Indian Ocean, in Mombasa, Kenya. A voice rises from a minaret: Allahu akbar.
The light moves west, and the call moves with it: to Khartoum and Cairo along the Nile, across the Sahel to Kano and the old towns of the Niger, and at last to Dakar, on the Atlantic.
Different accents, different melodies, the same words. A continent of mosques, some of them with stories you've walked through over these last days. Today: Islam in Africa today.

teach.b: Africa's story with Islam began with refugees welcomed in Abyssinia in the Prophet's own lifetime. And the voice that carried the call to prayer in Medina has an African story too.
A hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud tells how the words of the adhan came to a companion in a dream, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told him to teach them to Bilal, because Bilal's voice carried.
Bilal, remembered by tradition as a man of Abyssinian descent, freed from slavery, stood up and called the believers to prayer. The same words are called today. And Islam in Africa is not one thing.

It's the Sufi orders of Senegal, with their great gatherings. It's Qur'an schools in northern Nigeria where children sit with wooden boards. It's al-Azhar in Cairo, teaching students from many countries.

It's the stone mosques of Lamu and the mud mosque of Djenné. It's recitation: Egyptian reciters like Abdul Basit Abd al-Samad and Mahmoud Khalil al-Husary, whose recordings are still played far beyond Egypt.
The Qur'an names this kind of variety as one of God's signs.
In Pickthall's translation, among His signs is "the difference of your languages and colours."
Africa prays in Wolof, Hausa, Swahili, Somali, Amharic and Arabic, and stands in the same rows.
That closes the part on Africa: the first refuge, Egypt and the Nile, the Sahara, Mali and Mansa Musa, Timbuktu, Djenné, Songhay, the Swahili coast, Harar, and Nana Asma'u.

how: Across Africa, Muslims answer the adhan at each time of prayer in mosques large and small, and recordings of African reciters are shared and listened to around the world.

o: the first prayer of the day

games.q: Islam in Africa today — tap the pairs.
p: taught the adhan; his voice carried

s: Islam in Africa is one single style
Sufi orders, Qur'an schools, al-Azhar, stone and mud mosques: it takes many forms.
a hadith says the Prophet had the adhan taught to Bilal because his voice carried

games.q: the words of the call to prayer have just come to a companion in a dream. who should call them out?
games.why: in the hadith of Sunan Abi Dawud, the Prophet tells the companion to teach the words to Bilal, because Bilal's voice carried.

practice: If you can, put on a recording of a reciter from Egypt, Senegal, Nigeria, Sudan or anywhere on the continent, quietly; if not, sit in silence and remember a voice you've heard.

Don't try to understand every word: listen to the breath between the verses, and let your own breath slow to meet it. If you pray, let the recitation carry you; if not, simply listen, the way you'd listen to the sea.

wordCard.voice: Adhan. The call to prayer, carried today from Dakar to Mombasa over a continent of Muslims praying in many languages and standing in the same rows. Today's word.
